title: The NEW Tesla Roadster: My Honest Reaction
suggestedQueries: What's MKBHD's honest reaction to the new Roadster?
Will the Roadster ever be street-legal?
How does the fan-powered downforce work?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Okay, so... wow. So last night, Tesla had one of maybe maybe the... most... insane product demos of all time. It had a completely redesigned, brand new... cyber-looking... car, then it had a car driving up a wall, then an upside-down car, then a flying car, then a car that jumps and does a kickflip, and then a 0.6-second... 0 to 60. And yet realistically, a lot of this stuff was... a distraction from the facts and figures that we got...

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: the next morning, today, on the actual Tesla Roadster itself. So I guess if part of my job for the last decade has been watching and attending these tech events and deciphering... what's real versus... what you should pay attention to, what is fluff, then I figured I should definitely do this one. So RIP to the 2020 Tesla Roadster. You'll be missed... even though you never existed. But yeah, we've got a lot to talk about. Also, I hope the weather holds up 'cause it looks like it may rain at some point, but my fingers are crossed.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: So anyway, yeah, a lot of people... after last night... were freaking out and rightfully so... 'cause it was... pretty insane. A lot of people were also very skeptical and rightfully so, because it was pretty insane. But I think as there is with a lot of this stuff, there was actually... a bit of nuance to it. I think a good amount of what we saw last night at the Tesla Roadster event was, it was actually really cool. It was stuff that a lot of car people are at least interested in from an engineering perspective and were looking forward to. And then a lot of other parts of it... were completely insane... that...

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: I don't think we will ever see in person. So at the event itself, they started by just re-unveiling the Tesla Roadster... It's completely redesigned. It looks nothing like the one that was originally on stage back in 2017. And this thing looks like some sort of a... cyberified interpretation of a Lamborghini, maybe a Murciélago, if I'm being generous. It's very minimal, very... angular. It's got these... triangle shapes, these slot headlights. The doors go up now instead of going out. There's a headlight bar at the front and a taillight bar at the back, very Cybertruck and modern EV.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And then the back just has a lot going on: a huge moving wing, it has exhaust tips, which might seem a little crazy on an electric car, but that will make a lot more sense in a second. Me personally, I don't really love this new design, at least my first impression. I actually think the old car was quite pretty, even though it never existed. I thought that design was really cool and I was looking forward to it. This one, eh, some parts of it yes, some parts of it no. It's gonna take some time to grow on me, and trust me, it'll have time to grow on me. But then there's all the other capabilities... to talk about. So first thing it does is start to drive... up a wall slowly.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: It just approaches it and it starts to get a more and more impossible angle, and then it just drives straight up a wall until... it's completely upside down. It's stuck to this ramp like 60 feet in the air and is producing over 4,000 kilograms of downforce while not driving, not moving. This is basically revealing that it's a fan car, which we have seen before, but we'll get to that in a second. But then it goes back up that ramp again, and then the second time it goes up, it literally vaults off the top and does this insane flip maneuver, spinning around and then landing on the ground tires down. So clearly... there are...

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: thrusters all around the car pointed in all directions that are powerful enough to move the entire car in space, and then there's enough compressed air somewhere as a source to get the car to flip and then land softly and drive away... This is insane, obviously. So first of all, this was an... autonomous demo. This is a pre-scripted— there's no real human in the car, but it's a pre-scripted sort of robotic demo, probably for safety purposes. Think of it kind of like a... Boston Dynamics robot. It's capable of that, but this is like your best-case scenario and like the coolest thing they could possibly make it do. But then yeah, a lot of the thoughts you're having in your head about like, is this even possible?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Is this legal? Why would I want a car to do this? All of those are, I think, perfectly reasonable thoughts to have. It's also a pretty insane, radical, never-before-seen flying... car demo. that left a lot of questions unanswered. So... both things can be true. But really the strange thing to me is that this event, hosted by Tesla, doesn't really answer most of these important questions for people curious about the product... But then the next morning, today, we get at least 3 different videos from MotorTrend and Hagerty and Top Gear that combined with the newly refreshed Tesla website...

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: have helped us understand a lot more about what's actually happening here. So let's just break it down... What they didn't say at the event is there are 4 versions of this Roadster. There's the base, the Performance, the Thrust, and... Rocket specs. So the base car just sounds like, you know, the basic EV by itself with none of the frills, none of the party tricks. It's not even mentioned on the website. This is just what I heard from Franz in the MotorTrend video. But he said there's a base one that has none of the extra stuff. Then the Performance version of the Roadster...

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: is this car with a fan system... for downforce... So no cold gas thrusters yet, but the fan car is already... an absolutely insane idea. If you've been in the car world for a little bit, you've probably already heard about this little project, this little car called... the McMurtry Spéirling. And that thing... is... a single-seater, fully electric car with this whole fan system underneath and behind it. And it is absolutely insane. Obviously, the amount of grip you have while driving is super important to how well the car can handle, right?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: So for many years, we've seen this steady improvement... in sports cars, just improving aerodynamically because as the car reaches higher speeds, you have tons of air passing over the car and it can redirect that air up or down to push the car down into the ground. This is all about getting more grip. So instead of losing traction, pushing the car down in the ground helps keep it stuck so you can actually turn more aggressively... and not lose grip... You ever put your hand out the window on the highway like this and the air moves your hand up and down? Same idea... The car has different shaped pieces that help push the car down, but that only works at higher speeds, right?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: So if you want that same level of downforce at lower speeds, the idea of a fan car or the fan system is to put a fan that's connected... to some low-pressure area underneath the car that sucks the air out from under the car, creates a low-pressure zone so that the air above the car pushes it down. So that is what the McMurtry Spéirling is doing. It literally drops down a skirt underneath the car to create a little vacuum-sealed area, and it spins a fan at the back of the car... at a ridiculously high RPM. And that duct system basically keeps the car firmly planted to the ground...

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: It generates more downforce... than the actual weight of the car, which is why, yes, they've already done the driving upside down stunt. Maybe it didn't get as much PR, but... that's how much force this system generates. So it's... unbelievably capable on a track. There's a bunch of videos of it smoking the fastest high-downforce track cars in the world... around low-speed corners, literally driving around a GT3 RS, just absolutely nuts. That extra downforce makes the biggest difference at the lowest speeds.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: So from a launch from 0 to 60, it can put... all of its power down immediately, which is over 1,000 horsepower. And the McMurtry does 0 to 60 miles an hour in 1.4 seconds. Just shoots out in 1.4 seconds. It's crazy... And so there's videos of this thing going to different tracks and basically demolishing every lap record... everywhere they go because this thing finds grip... in places that other cars don't. It is genuinely one of the coolest science fair project cars that the world has ever seen.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: I kind of still want to get to drive one at one point. That'd be awesome. And so the Tesla Roadster inherits this fan system, and so it also inherits a 1.6-second... 0 to 60, which is nuts. And I'm I'm on the fence about whether or not... this could be street legal. I mean, I guess the law is the law. It's either legal or it isn't. But like there are lots of roads... where you probably would not want to use this system... because... there are potholes... and bumps and imperfections and things like that. So the skirts on the Spéirling... and the Roadster are made from like rubber and they're flexible and they're easily replaceable when they inevitably get worn out from dragging along the ground.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: But still, like the car has fans at the back, it literally hoovers up anything that's on the road under the car. And so it needs filters down there so large items don't get caught up in the fans. And the smaller pieces like little bits of gravel actually do make it through the fan system and shoot out the back. So if you are driving behind a fan car... while the fan is spinning, lots of air and lots of little debris is literally shooting out the back of it. So the McMurtry, I don't think is street legal with the fans running, but they also have said they're working on a street legal version. So very curious about that. It also depends on where the laws are, where you're driving.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Tesla is calling this Performance trim... "road ready" in their language. So it seems like they're ready to have this car or this version, this trim of the car be street legal... If it's not, you can expect to see it like GPS locked to just tracks or... drag strips and stuff like that. But then there's the next version of the trim, which is called "Thrust." That version of the car will have a fan system... already. And then it will also add thrusters to the back of the car. So at the back of the Roadster, you see these 4 fans... at the bottom.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: That's the suction system. Then the 4 bigger exhaust pipes at the top, that is the thrust system. And that's where it starts to get crazy because... those pipes... are attached to... a... 200-liter carbon-overlaid pressure vessel. When it's full, it's carrying 100+... kilograms of pressurized nitrogen... at 10,000 PSI right behind the driver's head, this little ball. And and that is insane... It's just objectively... completely insane.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: But that is how they combined with the fan system are able to achieve a sub-1-second 0 to 60 in that car. 'Cause you're you're past the limit of traction on tires at this point. You're just, you're strapping yourself to a little mini rocket and just, just, just gone. They showed demo videos of this at the event... Tons of compressed nitrogen coming out the back. It's pulling a couple of Gs and yeah, literally hits 60 miles an hour before it goes the length of a driveway. Some quick back-of-the-napkin math: that's like 3 Gs, 3 lateral Gs, which is crazy to experience in a car. Most cars, the limit of grip on tires is typically like 1.2, maybe 1.3 Gs. So that's nuts.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And you know, roller coasters do 3 Gs. It's not like... dangerous to your body, but it's just holding your arms up to the steering wheel will be 3 times harder than it normally would be. This one, again, not sure about... street legalness... You know, at the event they did this demo... hundreds of feet away from people and gave them hearing protection because those thrusters are incredibly loud on top of the already loud fans. There are definitely laws about how loud cars are allowed to be in certain places to pass regulations and actually be shipped...

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And so that will come into factor here. There's also like, there's lots of cars that like if you stand right behind a, you know, a quad exhaust, like a C8 Corvette and they rev it, like it'll burn your legs. So there's lots of crazy stuff happening in the sports car world already. But actually what I'm most concerned about is crash test... safety. Like cold gas thrusters and massive, carbon-overlaid compressed air canisters. It's great with rockets, I understand that, but rockets don't get crash safety tested like cars because if a rocket crashes, it's kind of—... that's kind of it, right?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Um, but what happens in the event of a safety incident when you have a massive balloon of 10,000 PSI compressed air next to your head? I just, I don't know what the plan is there. But anyway, the last spec, the last... promised spec is the... "Rocket" spec. And so this levels up again. So... it still has the fans at the bottom, it still has the thrusters at the back, but it adds... 6 more thrusters around the car facing various directions.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And it also adds one... massive 400-liter compressed air tank in... like the passenger seat area. So it becomes a one-seater. But anyway, all this extra compressed gas and all this extra thrusting will allow the party trick that we saw from the event, like jumping or doing a... massive kickflip over a 40-foot section of road for some reason, all of that stuff. Oh, and it'll do a 0 to 60... in 0.6 seconds, which sounds painful.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: This is pretty clearly... never going to be street legal. And I mean, that much is already clear on their website. They've already said it's not approved for public road use. But you can also only get... this car via... invite, which is a perfect little segmentation on their website to avoid... the liability of ever having to sell this to... a group outside of a very, very, very limited number of people. And I think... that that's why this event felt so weird to me because they basically went all in... on this insane demo, which to their credit, it was an insane demo.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And there was a ton of engineering that went behind it, probably many, many months... and months of trial and error... I mean, imagine being told by your boss you need to make a fan... car that can drive up the side of a building, but also... upside down and then fly off a wall and land on its wheels. Like, that's just a stupid amount of work that essentially amounts to a party trick. Like a really, really crazy, futuristic, insane engineering party trick... But is it even a party trick?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Like, can you do this in your driveway? Are you allowed to... have your car take off and fly 40 feet? Like, where... are you... even... able to do this? There's some talk about whether or not it was a real full-weight car that did the demo... And I mean, I don't know, if I was in charge, I'd be pulling some strings, like using a smaller battery and just doing anything I can to make sure it doesn't go horribly wrong. But that almost doesn't even matter. I think the... craziness of how extreme... that this event... was and how all in they went on this... crazy party trick was both figuratively... and literally smoke and mirrors in front of abandoning the old Roadster that spent some unknown amount of time in development and is now just never coming out.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Now, this one is supposed to be 2028. That's the new promise. That's what they said on stage. But then it kind of just... ended. Like, there wasn't really much more information after the crazy demos. And if you didn't watch anything else, then you'd miss a lot of other interesting engineering about the Roadster that started to show up in the videos this morning on things like Top Gear and the MotorTrend video that I talked about. Like, did you know this new Roadster's supposed to be... all... carbon fiber body panels and weigh... under 1,700 kilograms?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Like that, that's... 1,700 kilograms is less than this car! This car is a gas car, has a gas tank. Batteries are typically incredibly heavy and EVs are typically incredibly heavy... This car weighs more somehow... than their promised Roadster. Did you know that the new Roadster is supposed to have... just... rear-wheel drive? Usually these cars are incredibly fast because they're all-wheel drive. And the Roadster is just rear-wheel drive for the driving engagement... And so all of the 1,300 horsepower and 1,400 Newton-meters of torque...

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: come from the new dual motors at the rear, which are also now smaller and more power-dense than even what we saw in Plaid. The range... went... way down... from 600 miles to just... a promised 300+, but they also talked about 500-kilowatt supercharging, which would be the fastest we've seen in the US at the new V4 Superchargers, 15... to 80%... charge in 10 minutes. Did you know what they're promising with this Roadster? 25 to 30 minutes of full-on... maximum power, max attack track mode driving... That's also pretty rare...

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: for an EV. Typically, thermals and thermal management get in the way of that, but you could do legitimately multiple laps before you have to recharge, but then recharge quickly. It's a little more reasonable to expect this to be a car that actually sees a track someday. There's a whole bunch of active aero bits. There's a charging port behind the rear wing. There is a movable pedal box... There's a double wishbone suspension, brake-by-wire, steer by wire. The windows are tinted with a gold accent color to mimic a spacesuit visor. Like, there's just so much going on with this car.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: So like, if you're gonna do a new unveiling for a car that you've apparently spent a bunch of development time and... resources and hours on, I would've personally preferred if you showed that instead of spending... so much time... on... just the party trick and then... no extra information. But instead, here we are... all now distracted by the, like, rocket thruster stuff and the, like, at one point they said it was gonna go half the speed of sound, which come on, like it's, I'm pretty sure it's not gonna do that.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: The thrust mode is over in 3 to 5 seconds and then the tank is empty. So it's basically one-time use before you have to refill it, which in the Hagerty video they said would take 6 to 7 hours to refill. And the rocket thing, you know, doing a kickflip, incredible demo, you gotta admit. If literally any other company did that demo, we'd all be shocked. But... aside from being a really cool engineering demo, that to me doesn't have any other connection to, like, real-world performance benefit... The fan stuff, it does.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Obviously, more downforce and more grip equals... better cornering and handling and faster lap times. It makes perfect sense. That's why we've been seeing this on other cars. Even the thrusters at the back, you could say, okay, that's like a cool straight-line... drag race... gimmick, one-time thing. Fine. You could make an argument for... safety... in extreme braking events for, like, putting the thrusters on other parts of the car, but the kickflip over something... and the... jumping down off of the... ramp, I mean, that, it's just distracting.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And let's be real, do you really want the... people that you see on the highway every day when you commute with cars that are able to jump when they don't have a pilot's license? So... yeah, I guess marketing is marketing, and they have, in fact, abandoned the car... that they initially had spent some number of years out of the past 9 years developing. I don't know how I would feel... if I had been... in for some amount of money this entire time... and just saw the car completely change like that. But hey, to their credit, the referral reward free Roadster is still in my account...

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: and with the updated picture. So... I guess maybe... that is still happening. Maybe I'm still getting it. I don't know. Get subscribed to see that... I will keep you guys... posted. But I guess that actually brings us to the last question, which is just, will they actually—this is the big question they ended with... They're gonna ship in 2028 is what they, of course they promised it on stage. Will they actually ship this thing by 2028? Starting to sound familiar. So... the flying one... with the rocket one, no. That there's just no way... you or I... will ever be able to buy this car.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Of course, it's conveniently invite-only. We might as well ignore this ever becoming a real product. The base one, the fan car one even, I can see that actually, yes, being possible. But at this point, I actually don't even think it matters... because... Tesla has proven to us by now... that the Roadster is by far their least important product. Like, McMurtry... has been putting in a ton of public development work for this fan car idea. It doesn't surprise me one bit that... Tesla can come in and sort of big-brother them and all the other fan car concepts that came before them and use their bigger bankroll to try to bring it to life.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: But we shouldn't ignore that there's a reason that this... 2020 Roadster went... 9 years and never actually came... out, never actually existed. It's because it doesn't make a difference to the company if it comes out or not. It makes no difference to their bottom line. It's so low volume. Matter of fact, they actually recently killed Model S... and Model X, which are very well-known cars, because they also weren't selling enough to make a difference to the bottom line. They have priorities... like Model 3 and Model Y and the humanoid robot stuff they plan on in the future.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: You think they care about Roadster? Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, Yeah, shame on me. I'm not gonna be holding my breath for this to suddenly become a priority... for them to... start picking things up and shipping this thing right on time. But this event, given how much everyone is talking about it, was clearly a successful... engineering exercise... and marketing stunt. It's really what it is. A few months of incredible engineering, a demo that no one has... ever seen before. That's enough material to talk about Tesla for another few years.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: I was actually just digging into my account to see... what was going on with the Roadster... There's a Tesla Roadster reservation agreement. There's a nice little bullet point, number four, that reads that you understand that the Roadster is still under development at the time you enter into this agreement, so we cannot guarantee when your vehicle will actually be delivered or if... it will be delivered. Very interesting. You know, I think the take from Henry Catchpole at the end of the... Hagerty video is actually really... fair, which is, you know, it seems like Tesla's realized that just a really, really fast electric car doesn't really do it for people... anymore.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Like, it's old news. We've seen that by now, and they already make Plaid, so—... or made Plaid. So they abandoned it and swapped it out for something that kind of does do it for some people anyway, which is the dream of a flying car... It's this fun idea, and it makes way more headlines. And even if they never ship the thing, then that successful engineering exercise is at least a spectacle that we can talk about as a marketing success. So yeah, thanks for watching. And for more car-focused videos and thoughts on cars, get subscribed to the Auto Focus channel.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And if you do end up seeing a Tesla Roadster review, that's where it'll be. Catch you guys in the next one. Peace.

title: How We Make Money on YouTube with 20M Subs
suggestedQueries: How does Kurzgesagt make most of its money?
How much do YouTube ads actually pay them?
Does Bill Gates influence their videos?
How did the channel get started?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: In 2023 Kurzgesagt has existed for 10 years, insanely long in internet years. We are among the largest sciency channels on Youtube and still a bit of a black box to people. So let us talk about ourselves a bit in three parts: Our backstory, how we finance our work and the values of Kurzgesagt! Let’s jump to a more innocent time. From humble beginnings to Today Kurzgesagt’s foundation was laid when Philipp, our founder, dropped out of high school as a teenager.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Learning seemed daft and useless and he was not interested in anything. Until a very special teacher at a school for dropouts grabbed him by the neck. The way she taught was different. She talked about connections and the big picture. She told a story. For the first time ever, Philipp wanted to learn more without being forced. It was a key life experience. Kurzgesagt tries to recreate this experience for you. Nothing is boring if you tell a good story and we try to tell these stories, to spark excitement and make you want to go on and learn more.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Because of the one teacher that could do this, Philipp got a high school degree, studied history and design and eventually started Kurzgesagt as a passion project, inspired by Crash Course World history. In 2012 Youtube was less commercial and more idealistic. You couldn’t make a living with videos as involved as ours and that was fine. The goal was creative freedom and so for the first few years, it actually cost money to make Kurzgesagt. We had no outside funding, just intrinsic motivation and a few friends from university. We worked for clients during the day and on Kurzgesagt at night, 80-100 hours a week. It was a real struggle but also very rewarding.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: But then Patreon launched, sponsorships started, our views increased, Youtube changed. In 2015 the channel began to break even and then to earn a profit. But we were pretty burned out at this point, so we decided to bring in more friends and hire the first team members full time, creating a legal entity. More people meant that we could stop overworking, do more and improve. But we also needed to earn more; the livelihood of real humans depended upon it. None of us had any experience in running a company. We didn’t plan to become big or to grow – it sorta just happened.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: A decade later Kurzgesagt is not a small project anymore. We are an animation studio, with offices in Munich and Berlin. We need computers, monitors, tablets, desks, coffee, contracts, pay licences, taxes, rent and insurance. In 2023 our team consists of over 60 full employees and a lot of freelancers around the world. Salaries alone cost millions of dollars a year, just to stay around. This creates an interesting problem: with such high production costs, how can we publish our work for free?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: How we finance Kurzgesagt We have added up our earnings from 2015 through 2022. Our sources of funding change depending on opportunities and the state of the world. Early on, agency work was our main source of income, ad revenue varies, in some years we got more sponsorships than in others. The shop didn’t exist for a long time, then it became pretty big after we launched our calendar. 62% of our revenue comes indirectly or directly from you: You watch our videos with ads, support us on Patreon or buy from our shop.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: The single biggest source of income by far, is our shop that alone accounted for 40% over the last 8 years. The shop started small but once we published our calendar for the first time in 2016, we realised it could really help us do more things and we started producing more and more science products, from our posters to our gratitude journal or universe scented candles. YouTube ads accounted for 13% and Patreon 9%. So without your support we would cease to exist.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Our shop and Patreon are our most important sources of revenue, and because we see ourselves as science communicators – we don’t just do merch, but sciency products that we spend hundreds of hours researching, discussing with experts, polishing up and working on directly with the manufacturers. They are part of the science story we try to tell. It also just feels good to get directly funded by you guys and give you something back for it, on top of our videos. YouTube ads are a crucial part of our funding as well, but they are not within our control.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Then there is paid agency work, which we stopped doing in 2022 – it accounted for 9% of our revenue over the last 8 years. A lot in the beginning, not much by the end. Then there are commercial sponsors advertising products -they accounted for 12% of our revenue. We also got about 7% from German Public Broadcasting for the German Channel, but ended this partnership in 2022. Finally there are institutional sponsors representing about 10%. Some people take issue with this – especially Bill Gates has come under public scrutiny, and we’ve been criticised for even working with organisations funded by him. So let us look at this 10% in more detail: About 3% of our revenue over the last eight years came from the Gates organisations for a wide variety of topics, often suggested by us.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: 5% comes from Open Philanthropy and is only used for specific projects. With these funds, we have started Arabic, Hindi, Korean, Japanese, Portuguese, and French channels, bringing more free science content to more people. Then there is a two-year funding for original Tik Tok content, which gives us freedom to explore and learn how to do short form science communication. The final 2% came from other organisations like the red cross or the UN for example. We choose institutional sponsors carefully but if organisations want to fund videos that help us spread quality information about relevant topics, this is an easy yes for us, if we have the capacity for it. On top of that, the institutional sponsors we are working with align with our values.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: We have contracts with every grant giver or sponsor that bars them from editorial influence, other than suggesting topic areas like “global health” or “climate change”. We agree on video topics together, but sponsors can neither influence details, nor our conclusions. The final decision always remains with us. And usually, we develop the topics of the videos autonomously and tell the sponsor what we are doing afterwards. If you are interested in how we research our videos in detail, our head of research wrote an article about it.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Running an educational youtube channel is a balancing act that we take very seriously. We are doing our best to maintain this balance, adjusting whenever necessary. As a team and company we want to grow to give more people access to a science based outlook on the world. This brings us to our final topic – why are we doing Kurzgesagt? Our Values and Our Vision Our core mission is to spark curiosity. We want to make science and humanism accessible for as many people as possible. The effort we put into creating our videos is a way of achieving that – our videos are beautiful because that helps to spark curiosity, to understand complex topics, and because it just feels good to create and watch.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Our research is as intensive as it is so our videos are a good simplification of very complicated topics. We want to make people excited about science so they rediscover subjects they hated in school and see how amazing they are. On top of curiosity, we want to inspire long term thinking and a positive, constructive outlook. Being optimistic about the future of humanity is not mainstream and we think this is horrible. Pessimism often sounds smart and gets more views while optimism can sound naive but this is a bias that is not helpful for us as a species.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: So despite the gloominess of many topics, we want to approach them with informed and well researched optimism – not brushing humanity's very real challenges aside, but also not falling into the trap of pessimism. We want to inspire you to dream a little about the glorious future that we could actually build – but only if we believe it is possible. In the long run we don’t only want to do this on Youtube. The idea is for Kurzgesagt to be a positive influence across more media. On our Tik Tok channel, in the long form content we are exploring, in apps, in the VR game that will be released later this year and the games we plan to make in the future. Our shop is a central part of this vision: we start our stories with a video and end them with a pos ter.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: There are so many things we want to do. And thanks to you watching this right now, we have the freedom to work to the best of our knowledge and ability. In the end, we hope you like what we offer and that we will be doing something worthwhile for as long as we exist. And hopefully, we’ll have a lasting impact by making science and learning more fun for as many people as possible. If you personally want to help us do this, you can watch and share our videos, check out our shop, become a patreon or give us an ad blocker exception. We exist because of you and you have no idea how much we appreciate that you are here. And hopefully we are less of a black box now. In any case. Doing Kurzgesagt for a decade has been a pretty crazy ride.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: So from the whole team – Thank you so much for being with us all these years.

title: Inside the Mind of a Master Procrastinator | Tim Urban | TED
suggestedQueries: What is the Instant Gratification Monkey?
When does the Panic Monster show up?
Why is procrastination without deadlines so dangerous?
What's the Life Calendar at the end of the talk?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: So in college, I was a government major, which means I had to write a lot of papers. Now, when a normal student writes a paper, they might spread the work out a little like this. So, you know -- (Laughter) you get started maybe a little slowly, but you get enough done in the first week that, with some heavier days later on, everything gets done, things stay civil. (Laughter) And I would want to do that like that. That would be the plan. I would have it all ready to go, but then, actually, the paper would come along, and then I would kind of do this.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: (Laughter) And that would happen every single paper. But then came my 90-page senior thesis, a paper you're supposed to spend a year on. And I knew for a paper like that, my normal work flow was not an option. It was way too big a project. So I planned things out, and I decided I kind of had to go something like this. This is how the year would go. So I'd start off light, and I'd bump it up in the middle months, and then at the end, I would kick it up into high gear just like a little staircase.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: How hard could it be to walk up the stairs? No big deal, right? But then, the funniest thing happened. Those first few months? They came and went, and I couldn't quite do stuff. So we had an awesome new revised plan. (Laughter) And then -- (Laughter) But then those middle months actually went by, and I didn't really write words, and so we were here. And then two months turned into one month, which turned into two weeks.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And one day I woke up with three days until the deadline, still not having written a word, and so I did the only thing I could: I wrote 90 pages over 72 hours, pulling not one but two all-nighters -- humans are not supposed to pull two all-nighters -- sprinted across campus, dove in slow motion, and got it in just at the deadline. I thought that was the end of everything. But a week later I get a call, and it's the school.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And they say, "Is this Tim Urban?" And I say, "Yeah." And they say, "We need to talk about your thesis." And I say, "OK." And they say, "It's the best one we've ever seen." (Laughter) (Applause) That did not happen. (Laughter) It was a very, very bad thesis. (Laughter) I just wanted to enjoy that one moment when all of you thought, "This guy is amazing!"

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: (Laughter) No, no, it was very, very bad. Anyway, today I'm a writer-blogger guy. I write the blog Wait But Why. And a couple of years ago, I decided to write about procrastination. My behavior has always perplexed the non-procrastinators around me, and I wanted to explain to the non-procrastinators of the world what goes on in the heads of procrastinators, and why we are the way we are. Now, I had a hypothesis that the brains of procrastinators were actually different than the brains of other people.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And to test this, I found an MRI lab that actually let me scan both my brain and the brain of a proven non-procrastinator, so I could compare them. I actually brought them here to show you today. I want you to take a look carefully to see if you can notice a difference. I know that if you're not a trained brain expert, it's not that obvious, but just take a look, OK? So here's the brain of a non-procrastinator. (Laughter) Now ... here's my brain. (Laughter) There is a difference.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Both brains have a Rational Decision-Maker in them, but the procrastinator's brain also has an Instant Gratification Monkey. Now, what does this mean for the procrastinator? Well, it means everything's fine until this happens. [This is a perfect time to get some work done.] [Nope!] So the Rational Decision-Maker will make the rational decision to do something productive, but the Monkey doesn't like that plan, so he actually takes the wheel, and he says, "Actually, let's read the entire Wikipedia page of the Nancy Kerrigan/ Tonya Harding scandal, because I just remembered that that happened.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: (Laughter) Then -- (Laughter) Then we're going to go over to the fridge, to see if there's anything new in there since 10 minutes ago. After that, we're going to go on a YouTube spiral that starts with videos of Richard Feynman talking about magnets and ends much, much later with us watching interviews with Justin Bieber's mom. (Laughter) "All of that's going to take a while, so we're not going to really have room on the schedule for any work today. Sorry!" (Sigh) Now, what is going on here?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: The Instant Gratification Monkey does not seem like a guy you want behind the wheel. He lives entirely in the present moment. He has no memory of the past, no knowledge of the future, and he only cares about two things: easy and fun. Now, in the animal world, that works fine. If you're a dog and you spend your whole life doing nothing other than easy and fun things, you're a huge success! (Laughter) And to the Monkey, humans are just another animal species. You have to keep well-slept, well-fed and propagating into the next generation, which in tribal times might have worked OK.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: But, if you haven't noticed, now we're not in tribal times. We're in an advanced civilization, and the Monkey does not know what that is. Which is why we have another guy in our brain, the Rational Decision-Maker, who gives us the ability to do things no other animal can do. We can visualize the future. We can see the big picture. We can make long-term plans. And he wants to take all of that into account. And he wants to just have us do whatever makes sense to be doing right now. Now, sometimes it makes sense to be doing things that are easy and fun, like when you're having dinner or going to bed or enjoying well-earned leisure time.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: That's why there's an overlap. Sometimes they agree. But other times, it makes much more sense to be doing things that are harder and less pleasant, for the sake of the big picture. And that's when we have a conflict. And for the procrastinator, that conflict tends to end a certain way every time, leaving him spending a lot of time in this orange zone, an easy and fun place that's entirely out of the Makes Sense circle. I call it the Dark Playground. (Laughter) Now, the Dark Playground is a place that all of you procrastinators out there know very well.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: It's where leisure activities happen at times when leisure activities are not supposed to be happening. The fun you have in the Dark Playground isn't actually fun, because it's completely unearned, and the air is filled with guilt, dread, anxiety, self-hatred -- all of those good procrastinator feelings. And the question is, in this situation, with the Monkey behind the wheel, how does the procrastinator ever get himself over here to this blue zone, a less pleasant place, but where really important things happen? Well, turns out the procrastinator has a guardian angel, someone who's always looking down on him and watching over him in his darkest moments -- someone called the Panic Monster.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: (Laughter) Now, the Panic Monster is dormant most of the time, but he suddenly wakes up anytime a deadline gets too close or there's danger of public embarrassment, a career disaster or some other scary consequence. And importantly, he's the only thing the Monkey is terrified of. Now, he became very relevant in my life pretty recently, because the people of TED reached out to me about six months ago and invited me to do a TED Talk.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: (Laughter) Now, of course, I said yes. It's always been a dream of mine to have done a TED Talk in the past. (Laughter) (Applause) But in the middle of all this excitement, the Rational Decision-Maker seemed to have something else on his mind. He was saying, "Are we clear on what we just accepted?

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Do we get what's going to be now happening one day in the future? We need to sit down and work on this right now." And the Monkey said, "Totally agree, but let's just open Google Earth and zoom in to the bottom of India, like 200 feet above the ground, and scroll up for two and a half hours til we get to the top of the country, so we can get a better feel for India." (Laughter) So that's what we did that day. (Laughter) As six months turned into four and then two and then one, the people of TED decided to release the speakers.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And I opened up the website, and there was my face staring right back at me. And guess who woke up? (Laughter) So the Panic Monster starts losing his mind, and a few seconds later, the whole system's in mayhem. (Laughter) And the Monkey -- remember, he's terrified of the Panic Monster -- boom, he's up the tree! And finally, finally, the Rational Decision-Maker can take the wheel and I can start working on the talk. Now, the Panic Monster explains all kinds of pretty insane procrastinator behavior, like how someone like me could spend two weeks unable to start the opening sentence of a paper, and then miraculously find the unbelievable work ethic to stay up all night and write eight pages.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And this entire situation, with the three characters -- this is the procrastinator's system. It's not pretty, but in the end, it works. This is what I decided to write about on the blog a couple of years ago. When I did, I was amazed by the response. Literally thousands of emails came in, from all different kinds of people from all over the world, doing all different kinds of things. These are people who were nurses, bankers, painters, engineers and lots and lots of PhD students. (Laughter) And they were all writing, saying the same thing: "I have this problem too."

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: But what struck me was the contrast between the light tone of the post and the heaviness of these emails. These people were writing with intense frustration about what procrastination had done to their lives, about what this Monkey had done to them. And I thought about this, and I said, well, if the procrastinator's system works, then what's going on? Why are all of these people in such a dark place? Well, it turns out that there's two kinds of procrastination. Everything I've talked about today, the examples I've given, they all have deadlines.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And when there's deadlines, the effects of procrastination are contained to the short term because the Panic Monster gets involved. But there's a second kind of procrastination that happens in situations when there is no deadline. So if you wanted a career where you're a self-starter -- something in the arts, something entrepreneurial -- there's no deadlines on those things at first, because nothing's happening, not until you've gone out and done the hard work to get momentum, get things going. There's also all kinds of important things outside of your career that don't involve any deadlines, like seeing your family or exercising and taking care of your health, working on your relationship or getting out of a relationship that isn't working.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Now if the procrastinator's only mechanism of doing these hard things is the Panic Monster, that's a problem, because in all of these non-deadline situations, the Panic Monster doesn't show up. He has nothing to wake up for, so the effects of procrastination, they're not contained; they just extend outward forever. And it's this long-term kind of procrastination that's much less visible and much less talked about than the funnier, short-term deadline-based kind. It's usually suffered quietly and privately.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: And it can be the source of a huge amount of long-term unhappiness, and regrets. And I thought, that's why those people are emailing, and that's why they're in such a bad place. It's not that they're cramming for some project. It's that long-term procrastination has made them feel like a spectator, at times, in their own lives. The frustration is not that they couldn't achieve their dreams; it's that they weren't even able to start chasing them. So I read these emails and I had a little bit of an epiphany -- that I don't think non-procrastinators exist.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: That's right -- I think all of you are procrastinators. Now, you might not all be a mess, like some of us, (Laughter) and some of you may have a healthy relationship with deadlines, but remember: the Monkey's sneakiest trick is when the deadlines aren't there. Now, I want to show you one last thing. I call this a Life Calendar. That's one box for every week of a 90-year life. That's not that many boxes, especially since we've already used a bunch of those.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: So I think we need to all take a long, hard look at that calendar. We need to think about what we're really procrastinating on, because everyone is procrastinating on something in life. We need to stay aware of the Instant Gratification Monkey. That's a job for all of us. And because there's not that many boxes on there, it's a job that should probably start today. Well, maybe not today, but ... (Laughter) You know.

chunks.speaker: Speaker
chunks.text: Sometime soon. Thank you. (Applause)
